title: Systems, Linux, Windows & Networks
tagline: The machine, administered — Linux to RHCSA/RHCE, Windows Server, and networks with packet literacy.
blurb: IL-04 is the systems administration academy: Linux from first principles through the RHCSA EX200 performance exam (with LPIC as the vendor-neutral companion), Windows Server administration (identity, Group Policy, PowerShell), networking to Network+ N10-009 with Wireshark-level packet literacy, and RHCE EX294 Ansible automation. Performance exams are won in the terminal — every module pairs concept notes with original hands-on labs, timed troubleshooting scenarios, and a terminal simulator.

certifications.name: Red Hat Certified System Administrator (RHCSA)
certifications.trackCoverage: Module 1: EX200 performance-exam prep — SELinux, storage (LVM/Stratis/Btrfs/VDO), containers, troubleshooting under time.
certifications.note: EX200 is a hands-on lab exam. Confirm current objectives on redhat.com.

certifications.name: Red Hat Certified Engineer (RHCE)
certifications.trackCoverage: Module 4: EX294 Ansible automation — playbooks, roles, system roles, timed scenarios. Current RHCSA required.

certifications.name: CompTIA Network+
certifications.trackCoverage: Module 3: N10-009 full objective coverage with PBQ drills. Cross-links IL-09's core-stack module.

certifications.name: LPI LPIC-1 / LPIC-2
certifications.trackCoverage: Module 1: vendor-neutral companion track (101/102, 201/202) alongside the RHCSA path.

objectives: Administer Linux from first principles: filesystem, permissions, shell, systemd, storage, networking, SELinux.
Automate with bash and Ansible: idempotent playbooks, roles, and scheduled execution.
Administer Windows Server: NTFS, Active Directory, Group Policy, PowerShell, DNS/DHCP.
Troubleshoot networks by layer with packet-level evidence: addressing, switching, routing, wireless.
Pass performance exams (EX200/EX294) via timed hands-on scenarios — not multiple-choice cramming.

arc.title: First principles
arc.body: The shell as an instrument, the filesystem hierarchy, permissions, pipes and text processing. You learn to *think* in pipelines before you automate anything — because automation of a bad process just makes bad faster.

arc.title: Administration
arc.body: Users, systemd, storage (LVM/Stratis), networking, firewalls, SELinux on Linux; NTFS, AD, Group Policy, PowerShell on Windows. Two operating systems, one discipline: least privilege, documented change, verified state.

arc.title: Automation & proof
arc.body: Ansible playbooks and roles for RHCE; PBQ drills and timed scenarios for every performance exam. The exam is a workday compressed — you prepare by doing workdays.

modules.title: Linux Foundations to RHCSA
modules.summary: Linux from first principles through the RHCSA EX200 performance exam: filesystem hierarchy, permissions, the shell as an instrument, bash scripting, users/systemd/storage/networking/firewalls, SELinux, containers on RHEL — with LPIC-1/LPIC-2 as the vendor-neutral companion track.
objectives: Navigate and manipulate the filesystem hierarchy with pipeline fluency.
Manage users, groups, ACLs, systemd services, LVM/Stratis storage, and firewalld.
Apply SELinux contexts and troubleshoot denials.
Work EX200-style timed tasks: the exam is a workday compressed.

notes.title: First principles: the shell as an instrument
notes.body:
The **filesystem hierarchy** (`/etc` config, `/var` variable data, `/usr` programs, `/home` users, `/proc`+`/sys` kernel interfaces) is the map. **Permissions** (rwx × user/group/other, octal, setuid/setgid/sticky) are the law. **Pipes, redirection, and text processing** (`|`, `>`, `>>`, `grep`, `sed`, `awk`, `sort`, `uniq`, `xargs`) are the instrument.

- Think in pipelines: `journalctl -u nginx --since today | grep -i error | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr` — filter, extract, count, rank
- Permission math: `chmod 640` = rw-r-----; `chmod 4755` = setuid; know what each bit *does*, not just the number
- The shell is programmable: history expansion (`!!`, `!$`), brace expansion (`{a,b}`), globbing — speed is a feature
- `set -euo pipefail` in every script: exit on error, undefined vars, and pipe failures — the three lines that prevent 3 AM pages

notes.title: Administration: users, systemd, storage, network
notes.body:
**Users/groups/ACLs**: `useradd`, `groupmod`, `setfacl`/`getfacl` for fine-grained access beyond owner/group/other. **systemd**: units, `systemctl enable --now`, `journalctl -u`, targets, timers as the modern cron.

**Storage**: partitions (`parted`), **LVM** (PV → VG → LV — the layer that makes resizing sane), Stratis, Btrfs, VDO (deduplication/compression).

**Networking/firewalls**: `ip` (not `ifconfig` — it's 2026), `nmcli`, `ss -tlnp`, `firewalld` zones and rich rules.

- LVM mental model: physical volumes pour into a volume group; logical volumes are sliced out — resize any layer independently
- systemd unit anatomy: `[Unit]` (deps), `[Service]` (ExecStart, Restart=), `[Install]` (WantedBy) — read any unit file like a spec
- firewalld zones: assign interfaces to zones, open services not ports (`--add-service=http`), rich rules for exceptions

notes.title: SELinux and the performance exam
notes.body:
**SELinux contexts** (`user:role:type:level`) are the RHCSA's favorite trap: the file has the right Unix permissions but the wrong context, and the service is denied. `ls -Z`, `restorecon`, `semanage fcontext`, `audit2allow` (use sparingly — understand before allowing).

**Containers on RHEL**: `podman` (daemonless, rootless), quadlets for systemd integration.

**EX200 exam prep**: it's a *performance* exam — you get broken systems and a clock. Strategy:

- Read every task first, do the quick wins, flag the long ones
- `man` is available — know how to find, not memorize: `man -k`, `/` search
- Verify each task as you go: `systemctl is-active`, `sestatus`, test the service
- Troubleshooting under time: check the obvious (service running? port listening? firewall? SELinux?) in that order — the exam recycles the same five root causes
- LPIC companion: 101/102 (essentials) then 201/202 (advanced) — the vendor-neutral proof alongside the Red Hat one

cards.back: /etc: configuration. /var: variable data (logs, spool). /usr: programs and libraries.
setuid (4) + rwxr-xr-x: executes with the file owner's privileges.
PV (disks) → VG (pool) → LV (usable volumes). Resize any layer independently.

cards.front: SELinux denial with correct Unix perms: first check?
cards.back: ls -Z — the context is wrong. restorecon or semanage fcontext to fix.
Timers are systemd-native: logging via journal, dependencies, calendar or monotonic triggers. cron is simpler and universal.
TCP listening sockets with numeric ports and the owning process — the 'is it listening and who owns it' command.

quiz.q: A service fails to read /srv/data/file after a move from /home. Permissions are correct. Likely cause?
quiz.explain: mv preserves the source context (/home) — restorecon -Rv /srv/data fixes it. Classic RHCSA trap.

quiz.q: Which grows a filesystem online after extending its LV?
choices: resize2fs / xfs_growfs on the mounted fs
quiz.explain: LVM + online resize: lvextend then resize2fs (ext4) or xfs_growfs (XFS) — no downtime.

quiz.q: firewalld: allow HTTP persistently?
quiz.explain: Zone model: --add-service=http --permanent, then reload. Services, not raw ports.

quiz.q: set -euo pipefail guards against?
choices: silent failures: unchecked errors, unset vars, masked pipe failures
quiz.explain: -e exits on error, -u on unset variables, -o pipefail propagates pipe failures — the 3 AM page preventers.

quiz.q: podman vs docker, RHEL exam relevance?
choices: podman: daemonless, rootless, quadlets for systemd — the RHEL-native tool
quiz.explain: EX200 tests podman: rootless containers managed as systemd services via quadlets.

quiz.q: EX200 time strategy?
choices: read all, quick wins first, verify each, man pages allowed
quiz.explain: Triage like a workday: quick wins, flag long tasks, verify as you go, use man -k.

modules.title: Windows Systems Administration
modules.summary: Windows Server and desktop administration: installation and roles, NTFS permissions, services and the registry, event logs and diagnostics; identity with Active Directory (forests, domains, OUs, Group Policy, Kerberos/NTLM, hybrid); PowerShell automation (pipeline, remoting, DSC, modules); Windows networking services (DNS, DHCP, file/print, remote access).
objectives: Apply NTFS vs share permissions correctly — and explain the effective-access rule.
Design AD structure: forests, domains, OUs; deploy Group Policy deliberately.
Automate with the PowerShell pipeline: filter left, format right.
Run DNS/DHCP/file services and troubleshoot with event logs.

notes.title: Core: permissions, services, registry, logs
notes.body:
**NTFS permissions** (Full/Modify/Read&Execute/List/Read/Write) combine with **share permissions** — the effective access is the *most restrictive* of the two. This single rule answers half the permissions questions.

**Services** (`services.msc`, `sc.exe`, PowerShell `Get-Service`): startup types, dependencies, recovery actions. **Registry** (`HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services`): the configuration database — export before editing, always.

**Event logs and diagnostics**: Event Viewer (System/Application/Security), `wevtutil`, Reliability Monitor. Troubleshooting methodology: reproduce → check logs → isolate → fix → verify → document.

- Installation and roles: Server Core vs Desktop Experience (Core = smaller attack surface, the exam's preferred answer)
- NTFS special permissions: Traverse, Execute File, Read Attributes — know when the basic six aren't enough
- Effective access tab: use it — guessing permissions is how outages happen

notes.title: Identity: Active Directory
notes.body:
**Forests, domains, OUs**: forest (security boundary) → domains → OUs (delegation and Group Policy scope). Design OUs by *administration*, not by org chart.

**Group Policy**: GPOs link to sites/domains/OUs; processing order LSDOU (Local, Site, Domain, OU — later wins); enforcement vs block inheritance; `gpupdate /force`, `gpresult /r`.

**Authentication**: **Kerberos** (tickets: AS → TGS → service; time sync matters — 5-minute skew kills auth) vs **NTLM** (challenge-response, legacy, pass-the-hash risk). **Hybrid identity**: Entra ID Connect sync, SSO shapes.

- AGDLP for group nesting: Accounts → Global → Domain Local → Permissions — the exam's canonical pattern
- Kerberos needs: SPNs registered, time synced, KDC reachable — the troubleshooting trio
- Group Policy preferences vs policies: preferences tattoo lightly (can revert), policies enforce

notes.title: PowerShell and Windows networking
notes.body:
**PowerShell**: the **pipeline** passes *objects*, not text — `Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5`. Filter left (`Where-Object` early), format right (`Format-Table` last). **Remoting** (`Enter-PSSession`, `Invoke-Command`), **DSC** concepts (declarative configuration, LCM), script modules.

**Networking services**: **DNS** (zones, records, forwarders, scavenging), **DHCP** (scopes, reservations, failover), file/print services, remote access (VPN, DirectAccess successor thinking).

- Pipeline discipline: `... | Where-Object {...} | Select-Object Name,Status` — never `Format-*` before you're done processing
- DNS troubleshooting: `nslookup`/`Resolve-DnsName`, check forwarders, then scavenging/aging misconfigurations
- DHCP: 80/20 rule for scopes (legacy), or proper failover — know DORA (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge)

cards.back: Most restrictive wins. NTFS Full + Share Read = Read.
LSDOU: Local → Site → Domain → OU. Later wins (unless Enforced/Block).
Time skew >5 min, missing SPN, KDC unreachable.
Accounts → Global groups → Domain Local groups → Permissions. The nesting pattern.
Objects, not text — hence Where-Object/Select-Object instead of grep/awk.
Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — the four-packet lease dance.

quiz.q: NTFS Modify + Share Read on a folder. User's effective access?
quiz.explain: Most restrictive of NTFS and share wins: Read.

quiz.q: A GPO linked at Domain and OU conflict. Which wins (no enforcement)?
quiz.explain: LSDOU — later (closer to the object) wins; OU beats Domain.

quiz.q: Kerberos fails across the domain; clocks differ by 8 minutes. Fix?
quiz.explain: Kerberos tolerates ~5 min skew — 8 minutes breaks ticket validation. Sync time first.

quiz.q: Pipeline best practice?
choices: filter with Where-Object early, format last
quiz.explain: Filter left (reduce objects early), format right (formatting destroys the objects).

quiz.q: DNS resolves internally but not externally. Check first?
quiz.explain: Internal resolution works → the server is fine; external failure points at forwarders/root hints.

quiz.q: Server Core vs Desktop Experience for a new DC?
choices: Core — smaller attack surface, fewer patches
quiz.explain: Core is the exam's preferred answer: less surface, fewer reboots, fully manageable remotely.

modules.title: Networking Core: Network+
modules.summary: The Network+ N10-009 core with Wireshark-level packet literacy: OSI/TCP-IP models, IPv4/IPv6 addressing, subnetting to reflex, VLSM and summarization; switching/VLANs, routing protocols, wireless, appliances; security/operations, monitoring, the 6-step troubleshooting methodology, and packet analysis — plus PBQ drills and exam-day logistics.
objectives: Subnet IPv4 to reflex; explain IPv6 addressing structure.
Describe switching (VLANs, trunking) and routing (static, OSPF, BGP at concept level).
Read packets in Wireshark: identify handshakes, DNS, DHCP, TLS negotiation.
Apply the 6-step methodology to layered troubleshooting scenarios.
Beat Network+ PBQs: subnetting sims, CLI analysis, diagram troubleshooting.

notes.title: Models and addressing: the map
notes.body:
**OSI and TCP/IP**: seven layers vs four — use OSI as the *troubleshooting map* (isolate bottom-up: physical → data link → network → transport → up). **IPv4/IPv6**: v4 dotted-decimal and CIDR; v6 hex, prefix lengths, link-local (`fe80::/10`), global unicast, no broadcast (multicast instead).

**Subnetting** (to reflex): /24 = 254 hosts; borrow bits, compute ranges. **VLSM**: right-size each subnet (point-to-point links get /30 or /31, VLANs get what they need). **Summarization**: aggregate contiguous blocks (192.168.0.0/24–192.168.3.0/24 → 192.168.0.0/22).

- The 60-second drill: given any /25–/28, produce network/broadcast/usable range — trainable, tested
- IPv6 subnetting is *easier*: nibble boundaries (/48 site, /64 subnet) — hex makes it visual
- Summarization reduces routing tables — know when aggregation is valid (contiguous, same next hop)

notes.title: Implementation: switching, routing, wireless
notes.body:
**Switching/VLANs**: collision vs broadcast domains, VLAN tagging (802.1Q), trunk vs access ports, STP (loop prevention — know what a blocked port means). **Routing**: static vs dynamic; **OSPF** (link-state, areas, Dijkstra inside); **BGP** (path-vector, the Internet's routing protocol — AS_PATH in concept).

**Wireless**: 802.11 standards (a/b/g/n/ac/ax — frequency, MIMO, channel width), WPA2 vs WPA3, site-survey thinking (channels 1/6/11 on 2.4 GHz).

**Appliances**: firewalls (stateful vs NGFW), load balancers (algorithms: round-robin, least-connections), proxies, IDS/IPS placement.

- VLANs segment broadcast domains — trunk ports carry tagged multi-VLAN traffic
- OSPF converges fast within an AS; BGP carries policy between ASes — different jobs
- 2.4 GHz: only channels 1, 6, 11 don't overlap — the most-tested wireless fact in existence

notes.title: Security, operations, packets, PBQs
notes.body:
**Security concepts (14%)**: segmentation, NAC, VPN types (IPsec vs SSL/TLS), hardening network devices. **Monitoring**: SNMP, NetFlow/sFlow, baselines and anomaly detection — you can't troubleshoot what you don't measure.

**6-step troubleshooting methodology**: identify → theory → test → plan → implement → verify/document — same discipline as A+, applied to packets.

**Wireshark analysis**: follow the TCP stream, read the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), spot retransmissions (congestion/loss), decode DNS and DHCP exchanges, recognize TLS ClientHello.

**N10-009 exam prep**: PBQs are subnetting sims, CLI output analysis, and diagram troubleshooting — the drill set in the Labs tab rehearses exactly these. Objective-by-objective readiness: weight-driven (Troubleshooting 24% first).

cards.back: Physical → data link → network → transport → session → presentation → application. Cabling before configuration.
32 - 2 = 30. (/27 = 5 host bits = 32 addresses.)
802.1Q — trunk ports carry tagged frames for multiple VLANs.
OSPF: link-state, inside one AS, fast convergence. BGP: path-vector, between ASes, policy-driven.
1, 6, 11. Everything else overlaps.
SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Retransmissions in a capture mean loss/congestion.

quiz.explain: /27: 32 addresses, .64–.95; network .64, broadcast .95; usable .65–.94.

quiz.q: Summarize 10.1.0.0/24 through 10.1.3.0/24.
quiz.explain: Four contiguous /24s = /22 (22 network bits).

quiz.q: A switch port in STP 'blocking' state means ___.
quiz.explain: Blocking prevents loops; the port listens but doesn't forward user traffic.

quiz.q: WPA3's key improvement over WPA2?
choices: SAE handshake — resists offline dictionary attacks
quiz.explain: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals replaces the crackable WPA2 4-way handshake.

quiz.q: In a capture, many TCP retransmissions indicate ___.
quiz.explain: Retransmissions = segments not acknowledged — loss, congestion, or a dead peer.

quiz.q: First step when 'the network is down'?
choices: identify the problem: scope (one host? one VLAN? everyone?)
quiz.explain: Scope first — one host is a local issue; everyone is infrastructure. Methodology before tools.

modules.title: RHCE: Ansible Automation
modules.summary: Red Hat Certified Engineer EX294: Ansible automation on RHEL — inventory and patterns, playbooks and plays, variables and facts, idempotence as a discipline; roles and Galaxy, system roles, automation controller concepts, and timed performance scenarios. Current RHCSA required — this module assumes you can already administer the systems you're automating.
objectives: Write idempotent playbooks: inventory, plays, variables, facts, handlers.
Build roles; consume Galaxy and the RHEL system roles.
Reason about automation controller concepts: jobs, inventories, credentials.
Complete EX294-style timed scenarios: multi-system configuration under the clock.

notes.title: Ansible foundations: idempotence as a discipline
notes.body:
**Inventory and patterns**: INI/YAML inventories, groups, `webservers:&staging` patterns, `--limit`. **Playbooks and plays**: YAML lists of plays → tasks → modules. **Variables and facts**: precedence (extra vars win), `ansible_facts`, Jinja2 templating.

**Idempotence**: running twice changes nothing the second time — the *definition* of correct automation. Every task should be safe to re-run: `state: present` not shell commands that append blindly.

- Ad-hoc first: `ansible web -m ping`, `ansible web -m yum -a 'name=nginx state=present'` — prove the concept before writing the playbook
- Handlers: restart the service *only when the config changed* (`notify:`) — the efficiency pattern
- Facts: `ansible_facts['os_family']` for conditionals (`when:`) — one playbook, many distributions
- Vault: `ansible-vault encrypt` for secrets — never commit plaintext credentials

notes.title: Roles, system roles, controller
notes.body:
**Roles and Galaxy**: roles = reusable units (tasks/handlers/templates/files/vars); Galaxy = the sharing hub — vet what you download. **RHEL system roles**: Red Hat's supported roles (timesync, selinux, firewall, storage, network) — the exam expects these, not random Galaxy roles.

**Automation controller concepts**: inventories, credentials, job templates, workflows, RBAC — the enterprise scheduling and access layer over Ansible.

- Role structure is convention: tasks/main.yml, handlers/main.yml, templates/, defaults/main.yml — learn the layout once
- System roles are idempotent and tested — prefer them over hand-rolled equivalents on the exam
- Controller: know what a job template bundles (project + inventory + credentials + playbook) at concept level

notes.title: EX294: the timed performance exam
notes.body:
EX294 gives you **real RHEL systems and a clock**: configure them with Ansible to a specification. Strategy:

- Skeleton first: inventory + playbook structure + variable files, then fill tasks
- Test incrementally: `--check --diff` (dry run) before the real run; `--limit` to iterate on one host
- Idempotence is graded: re-run your playbook and confirm zero changes
- Time management: read the entire spec, do the deterministic tasks first, leave debugging for the end
- Current RHCSA required — the exam assumes you know *what* to configure; it tests *how* you automate it
- Common traps: YAML indentation, quoting Jinja2 in `when:` (don't double-wrap `{{ }}`), forgetting `become: true`

cards.back: Running twice changes nothing the second time. The definition of correct automation.
Only when a notifying task reports 'changed' — e.g., restart nginx only if the config changed.
Extra vars (-e) beat everything. Know the order for debugging surprises.
System roles are Red Hat-supported (timesync, selinux, firewall...) — prefer them on the exam.
Dry run showing what WOULD change — the pre-flight for every playbook run.
when: ansible_facts['os_family'] == 'RedHat' — no {{ }} wrapping; when: already evaluates Jinja2.

quiz.q: A task using shell: echo x >> /etc/motd is ___.
choices: not idempotent — appends on every run
quiz.explain: >> appends every run — use copy/template with content: for idempotence.

quiz.q: Restart nginx only when its config changed: mechanism?
quiz.explain: notify: restart nginx on the config task; the handler runs once, only on change.

quiz.q: Target webservers except staging: pattern?
quiz.explain: ! excludes — webservers:&staging would intersect instead.

quiz.q: Secrets in a playbook: correct handling?
quiz.explain: ansible-vault encrypts at rest; decrypt at runtime with --ask-vault-pass or a vault password file.

quiz.q: Task needs root on remotes: add?
quiz.explain: become: true (privilege escalation) — the modern, correct directive.

quiz.q: Playbook ran green but changed nothing on re-run: verdict?
quiz.explain: Zero changes on re-run is the goal — that's idempotence proven.

scriptLabs.title: LVM: Build, Extend, Grow — Online
scriptLabs.brief: Script the full LVM lifecycle: PV → VG → LV → filesystem → extend → online grow. Use loop devices so it's safe anywhere. Required fragments force the layer order.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# Use a file-backed loop device as our 'disk'
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256
DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img)
echo "disk: $DEV"
# TODO: pvcreate, vgcreate vgdata, lvcreate -n applv -L 100M, mkfs.xfs, mount, then extend + xfs_growfs
scriptLabs.hint: pvcreate $DEV && vgcreate vgdata $DEV && lvcreate -n applv -L 100M vgdata && mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/applv. Extend: lvextend -L +100M /dev/vgdata/applv && xfs_growfs /mnt/app.
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256
DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img)
pvcreate "$DEV"
vgcreate vgdata "$DEV"
lvcreate -n applv -L 100M vgdata
mkfs.xfs -f /dev/vgdata/applv
mkdir -p /mnt/app && mount /dev/vgdata/applv /mnt/app
df -h /mnt/app
# online extend: no unmount, no downtime
lvextend -L +100M /dev/vgdata/applv
xfs_growfs /mnt/app
df -h /mnt/app
# cleanup: umount /mnt/app; lvremove -y /dev/vgdata/applv; vgremove -y vgdata; pvremove -y $DEV; losetup -d $DEV

scriptLabs.title: Bash Hardening Audit Script
scriptLabs.brief: Write an audit script with set -euo pipefail that checks: passwordless sudo entries, world-writable files in /etc, listening ports without a known service, and failed SSH logins today. Output a findings report.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
REPORT=/tmp/audit-$(date +%F).txt
{
echo "=== hardening audit $(date) ==="
# TODO 1: sudoers without password (visudo -c friendly: grep NOPASSWD /etc/sudoers*)
# TODO 2: world-writable under /etc
# TODO 3: listening TCP ports (ss -tlnp)
# TODO 4: failed SSH logins today (journalctl)
} > "$REPORT"
echo "wrote $REPORT"
scriptLabs.hint: grep -R NOPASSWD /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/. find /etc -xdev -type f -perm -0002. journalctl -u sshd --since today | grep -i 'failed'.
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
REPORT=/tmp/audit-$(date +%F).txt
{
echo "=== hardening audit $(date) ==="
echo '--- NOPASSWD sudoers ---'
grep -R --include='*' 'NOPASSWD' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ 2>/dev/null || echo 'none found'
echo '--- world-writable in /etc ---'
find /etc -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -print 2>/dev/null || echo 'none found'
echo '--- listening TCP ---'
ss -tlnp
echo '--- failed SSH today ---'
journalctl -u sshd --since today 2>/dev/null | grep -ci 'failed' || echo 0
} > "$REPORT"
echo "wrote $REPORT"

scriptLabs.title: Ansible: Idempotent Web Tier
scriptLabs.brief: Write a playbook that installs nginx, deploys a templated index.html, opens the firewall, and enables the service — fully idempotent, with a handler. Then prove idempotence with a second run.
scriptLabs.starter:
---
- name: web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    # TODO: nginx present, index.html from template, firewalld http, service enabled+started, notify handler on template change
  handlers:
    # TODO: restart nginx
scriptLabs.hint: Use ansible.builtin.yum/dnf with state: present; template src -> dest notify: restart nginx; firewalld service=http permanent+immediate; service state=started enabled=true.
scriptLabs.solution:
---
- name: web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: nginx installed
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: nginx
        state: present
    - name: index deployed
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: index.html.j2
        dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
        mode: '0644'
      notify: restart nginx
    - name: http allowed
      ansible.posix.firewalld:
        service: http
        permanent: true
        immediate: true
        state: enabled
    - name: nginx running
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true
  handlers:
    - name: restart nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted
# prove it: ansible-playbook web.yml && ansible-playbook web.yml  # second run: 0 changed

options.text: Time sync: w32tm /query /status on DC and client

blocks.body: systemctl is-active <svc> → ss -tlnp (listening?) → firewall-cmd --list-all → ls -Z (SELinux?) → journalctl -u <svc> --since '10 min ago' → df -h (disk?)
chmod 640/750/644 · chown user:group · setfacl -m u:ana:rwx · getfacl · umask 027 → new files 640/750
pvcreate → vgcreate → lvcreate → mkfs → mount · extend: lvextend -r (auto-grows fs on some) or lvextend + resize2fs/xfs_growfs
getenforce · ls -Z · restorecon -Rv · semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?' · ausearch -m avc -ts recent
systemctl enable --now · systemctl status · journalctl -u <svc> -f · timers: OnCalendar=daily
Effective access = most restrictive (NTFS vs share) · GPO order LSDOU · gpupdate /force · Kerberos needs time+SPN+KDC · AGDLP nesting
Get-X | Where-Object {...} | Sort-Object | Select-Object -First N · filter left, format right · Invoke-Command for remoting
Scope first (one host? VLAN? all?) → bottom-up OSI → verify each fix → document. Packets don't lie: capture it.

answerBank.a: RHCSA if you want Red Hat-shop jobs (it's a performance exam — the strongest signal). LPIC-1 as the vendor-neutral companion; the overlap is ~60%, so the second costs little. This module prepares both in one pass.

answerBank.q: How do I beat SELinux instead of disabling it?
answerBank.a: Learn the three commands: ls -Z (see the context), restorecon (fix file contexts), semanage fcontext (persist the rule). Disabling SELinux on the exam fails the task; in production it removes a layer. The module's labs make contexts routine.

answerBank.q: NTFS or share permissions — which do I set?
answerBank.a: Both, deliberately: NTFS for the real security boundary (it travels with the file), share for the network entry point. Effective access is the most restrictive of the two — design with that rule, verify with the Effective Access tab.

answerBank.q: How do I get fast at subnetting?
answerBank.a: The 60-second drill in the trainer: random /25–/28, produce network/broadcast/usable range. Daily for two weeks. It's arithmetic reflex, not intelligence — everyone who practices gets fast.
You need lab time — containers or a VM with RHEL (developer subscription is free for individuals). The module's timed scenarios assume a lab; reading about Ansible doesn't pass EX294.

answerBank.q: Wireshark feels overwhelming — where to start?
answerBank.a: Three patterns: the TCP handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK), DNS query/response, DHCP DORA. Follow one TCP stream per session. The module's packet notes build from these three outward.
